title: Landfill Airspace Recovery Contractor
one_liner: Mine old landfill cells to recover airspace, not metals, and sell it to operators at a fraction of the cost of new capacity.
customer: Owners of landfills with under about 10 years of permitted capacity, in airspace-constrained markets: municipal and regional authorities, and independents in the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic and parts of the West.
problem: New landfill cells take years to permit and tipping fees in constrained markets often exceed $100 per ton. Insiders dismiss landfill mining because recovered metals and RDF are low value, so nobody prices the airspace.
solution: An airspace audit (drone LiDAR, borings, waste characterization) followed by a mobile trommel and ballistic-separator spread. It excavates old cells, screens fines for cover and fill, pulls metals and plastics, and re-places compacted residual. Contracts are priced per cubic yard of airspace recovered, compared to the cost of new capacity and haul-out. It skips cells with unknown PFAS risk until sampled.
why_now: Elevated commodity prices, cheaper vision sorting and robotics, tighter EPR and diversion rules that shrink incoming tonnage certainty, and PFAS liability pushing operators to characterize legacy cells anyway.
revenue_model: $25-75K audit fee, then $/CY of airspace recovered (or a share of avoided haul-out cost), plus a share of recovered commodities.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone prices the contents of the landfill. The scarce, regulated, appreciating asset is the airspace, and the true replacement lead time is 10 years.
first_30_days: Screen 20 landfills with under 7 years of remaining capacity using public permit data and satellite volumetrics. Offer free desktop screening and a paid audit of the oldest cell. Lease a trommel by the month rather than buying.

title: Lien-Release Chasing for Title Agents
one_liner: A per-release service that finds who now owns an old paid-off mortgage, sends the statutory demand, and chases the lender by voice, email and mail until the release is recorded.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and attorney closing offices, plus underwriters' curative departments. Priced per release delivered.
problem: An ALTA survey of 449 title professionals in 47 states (March 2026) found 59% name securing releases for prior mortgages as the most significant curative challenge. 60% of purchases need 3-5 title issues cleared before closing, over 90% involve mortgage payoffs, and 80%+ require reviewing at least 11 documents. HousingWire (September 25, 2026) reports search and exam is still mostly manual and files stall most on older or rural county records. A DataTrace study found generic public-record AI missed meaningful title matters in 40.8% of 200 searchable files, though that is a vendor study.
solution: Given a commitment with open-of-record mortgages, the system identifies the current holder or servicer from the chain of assignments, MERS servicer data and bank merger histories. It finds the right release department or statutory agent and sends a compliant satisfaction demand for that state. Voice agents work lender IVRs and phone queues, with email and certified-mail follow-up on a schedule. It monitors county recorder indexes and e-recording confirmations, uses lost-satisfaction affidavit routes where allowed, and posts a clear event back to the agent's title software. Human curative specialists take escalations such as executive letters to banks.
why_now: Title premiums hit $4.5B in Q1 2026 and volume rose nearly 14% in 2025, while ALTA says title costs fell about 5% even as operational demands and fraud work grew. Search-and-exam automation is crowded and improving (Qualia and others), which pushes the human bottleneck to the curative chase. Voice agents can now handle multi-turn calls with lender phone trees.
revenue_model: Fee per release delivered ($75-250 to test), success-only, plus a monthly minimum for agencies with steady volume. Upsell to underwriters as a curative-outsourcing vendor.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is automating search and exam, but the survey says the hardest part is the human chase for releases, which is phone- and letter-heavy, statute-driven and rules-based, and has no dominant product. Most states set deadlines and penalties for lenders that fail to record satisfactions, so a correctly formatted demand gets a response (statute detail is my domain knowledge and needs verifying by state). Evidence: ALTA study (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/alta-study-title-production-complexity-curative-work/), the manual search-and-exam story (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/title-search-exam-manual/), and the AI-miss study (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/public-record-linked-ai-misses-key-title-issues-in-many-searches/).
first_30_days: Sign 3 title agencies as design partners with their first 20 releases free. Have them share historic release requests to seed a database of the top 200 servicers and bank-merger successors. Build demand templates for the 10 highest-volume states and a voice agent for the top lenders' release lines. Start charging per release by day 30 and log turnaround days versus the agency's manual baseline.

title: Cure Desk: Medical-Bill Triage for Delinquent Tenants
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Real estate (office-to-resi, vacancy, property mgmt, affordability)
one_liner: A landlord-paid service that turns a late-rent notice into a medical-bill rescue, using hospital charity care, bill negotiation and coverage re-enrollment to free up the cash that pays the rent.
customer: Multifamily and single-family-rental operators (500-20,000 units) pay per cured account.
problem: 20% of renter households paid late or missed rent in 2025, and middle-income households jumped from 14.3% to 21.6%. About 4.8M people lost coverage after enhanced ACA subsidies expired. Landlords now face AI-assisted pro se tenant filings (41,000+ federal pro se cases in 2025) and increasingly conclude that cash-for-keys is cheaper than winning an eviction.
solution: When a resident is 3-5 days late, the property manager sends an opt-in text. If medical bills or a coverage loss are the cause, an advocate applies to the hospital's financial-assistance program (nonprofit hospitals must have one), negotiates the bill, sets payment plans and opens a special enrollment period. The landlord pays a success fee (roughly $300-500) only when arrears are cured, versus thousands per eviction.
why_now: Subsidy expiry created millions of self-pay patients in 2026, delinquency is at series highs, and the legal cost of eviction is rising with AI-generated filings. Medicaid churn from Jan 2027 will add more.
revenue_model: Success fee per cured account, with an optional $/unit/month retainer for early-warning outreach.
non_obvious_insight: A missed rent payment is the earliest and most reliable distress signal in consumer finance, and it lands on the one party with the data, scale and cash motive to pay someone to fix it. A tenant's hospital bill is far more negotiable than a landlord's arrears, so the fix comes from the health side.
first_30_days: Recruit two ex-hospital financial counselors. Sign two mid-size operators and run 200 delinquent accounts manually via SMS and a shared inbox. Track cure rate and cost per cure. Landlords pay only after cure.

title: Per-Class Portable Benefits for Fitness Instructors
angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
one_liner: A payout layer that skims a small per-class contribution from studios and class apps into each 1099 instructor's own injury income protection, health-premium credit and retirement account, structured to give studios legal cover under portable-benefits laws.
customer: Boutique studio groups with 5-30 locations, gym franchisees, class marketplaces and corporate-wellness providers that use 1099 instructors, paying $0.50-2 per class. Instructors opt in for bonus benefits. Trainer associations are a distribution channel.
problem: Several hundred thousand US fitness instructors and trainers work at 3-6 venues, mostly as part-time or self-employed workers with no disability cover, workers' comp or retirement plan. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired in 2026, federal-marketplace enrollment fell about 21%, and an estimated 4.8M people became uninsured, so self-employed instructors' premiums jumped. Injuries to voices, knees and backs end income immediately. Studios face misclassification suits, and because each studio has separate payroll, no one accumulates benefits.
solution: Integrate with scheduling systems (Mindbody, Momence, Walla) to read classes taught. Studios contribute a per-class amount into each instructor's benefits wallet, for example $1.25. The wallet buys short-term income protection through a partner insurer, an ACA premium top-up or HSA deposit, and an IRA contribution. Contributions follow the instructor across venues. The structure is designed to fit safe harbors in states that have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 (verify current list and get legal review).
why_now: ACA subsidy expiry hit self-employed workers in 2026. A handful of states have passed portable-benefits laws since 2023 that shield platforms from treating contributions as employment evidence. Class-pass economics keep instructors spread across venues. Misclassification exposure keeps studio owners nervous.
revenue_model: A platform fee of 8-10% of contributions, insurer commissions of 12-20% on income protection, and interchange on a benefits card. 10,000 instructors at $2,000 a year in contributions is $20M of flow and about $1.6-2M of revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Portable benefits have struggled with gig platforms because work units are messy. Fitness instructors' work is already itemized in software as class events, so a contribution per class is a natural unit. Fitness is the ideal beachhead because work is high-frequency, discrete, multi-venue and tracked, and instructors are health-literate and physically at risk, so they will value injury protection.
first_30_days: Sign one 10-studio group. Run contributions through a simple ACH from the studio. Partner with an existing accident and disability MGA for a $2-4 a week income-protection policy. Enroll 100 instructors and pilot a $1-per-class contribution. Track instructor retention at the studio and first claims. Target 500 instructors within six months.

title: Unstaffed Overnight ICU for Vet Clinics
one_liner: Radar-based contactless vitals and camera analytics let general practices keep IV-fluid and post-op patients overnight without a 24-hour staff, easing ER transfers and ER overload.
customer: 2-10 DVM general practices and low-cost clinics with a small treatment ward, plus shelter medical wards such as parvo units.
problem: With about 2 techs per vet, most clinics cannot staff nights, so hospitalized pets are transferred to 24-hour ERs at higher cost, sent home early or not treated. That drives owner cost, client loss and ER crowding.
solution: A low-cost mmWave radar puck per cage measures respiratory rate and motion, with a camera to watch IV lines and pumps. An on-site alert plus a pooled remote overnight RVT/DVM desk cover 20 clinics, with thresholds tuned by species and weight.
why_now: Consumer sleep-tracking made mmWave sensors cheap, edge vision models run on small devices, the tech shortage is structural, and the spectrum-of-care movement wants intermediate options between full transfer and no treatment.
revenue_model: $150 per cage hardware plus $79-149 per cage per month, and per-night remote-coverage fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone tries to automate diagnosis. The binding constraint is night hours: the lack of an awake person forces a general practice to hand revenue and clients to the ER. Monitoring substitutes for staying awake, not for the doctor.
first_30_days: Buy off-the-shelf radar and cameras and instrument 4 cages in 2 friendly clinics. Log respiratory-rate accuracy against manual counts for 30 nights. Sell $99-per-cage pilots and recruit pooled overnight RVT coverage.

title: Allergen Drift Alerts for School Cafeterias
one_liner: A weekly diff engine over the open Open Food Facts and USDA Branded Food Products data that tells school nutrition directors when a product on their order guide silently changed its allergens.
customer: K-12 school district food service directors and their purchasing co-ops and state agencies (about 13,000 US districts). A parent-facing paid alert tier for families of children with severe allergies is a secondary market.
problem: Distributors substitute products and manufacturers reformulate without notice. After sesame became the ninth major US allergen, some bakeries began adding sesame on purpose. Directors keep allergen lists in spreadsheets built from last year's spec sheets. Recalls are announced only after exposure, and cooks get blamed for what is really supplier drift.
solution: Ingest the district's order guide (Sysco, US Foods, Gordon Food Service item lists) and match SKUs to GTINs. Track ingredient statements and allergen declarations over time using Open Food Facts revision history and the monthly USDA Branded Food Products (GDSN) releases. Send a weekly 'allergen drift' report and immediate alerts when an allergen is added, a 'may contain' changes, or a substitution appears. Auto-update the district's allergen matrix and menu labels.
why_now: Branded-food data goes stale quickly and USDA now publishes monthly GDSN updates. Reformulation churn following the 2023 sesame rule and supply-chain substitutions is high. Open Food Facts has reached scale, and diffing it is cheap while no one sells the diff.
revenue_model: USD 500-1,500 per district per year, tiered by SKU count. State-agency or co-op bulk licenses. Parent alert tier at USD 3-5 per month.
non_obvious_insight: Most cafeteria allergen incidents trace to a silent supplier change, not to cooking error, so the value is monitoring the upstream data exhaust that already exists and is free. Directors will pay for peace of mind and liability evidence, not for a new database.
first_30_days: Build the diff pipeline for the 300 most common K-12 SKUs. Publish a free weekly 'Allergen Drift Report' newsletter aimed at food service directors and state school nutrition associations to build trust. Offer 5 districts a free SKU-matching of their full order guide. Convert to paid alerts with the first two districts that catch a real change.

title: Verification Service for Satellite Imagery Authenticity
one_liner: Check whether a satellite image is real, and issue a chain-of-custody certificate for images used as evidence.
customer: Trade-finance banks and collateral managers, property and cargo insurers, sanctions and compliance teams, and newsroom verification desks.
problem: Generative AI can now fake satellite images, and fakes circulated during conflicts in 2025 (prior knowledge). Imagery is increasingly used as evidence for loans against stockpiles, insurance claims, sanctions cases and environmental claims. Fraud incentives rise with that value, and nobody certifies pixels.
solution: A verification API that checks a submitted image against multi-provider archives (free Sentinel and Landsat plus commercial partners) and physical consistency (sun angle, shadows, sensor geometry). Partners can sign images at ingestion with a provenance manifest. Deliver certified 'as-of' extracts for legal use.
why_now: Generative image quality crossed the threshold in 2025-26. Imagery archives are large and multi-source, and providers are looking for premium 'verified' tiers. The briefing notes decision products for regulated buyers remain open.
revenue_model: $20-200 per verification. Enterprise subscriptions of $30-150k per year. Revenue share with imagery providers on verified tiers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection models age quickly, but archive access does not. The moat is a cross-provider archive and provenance partnerships, not a classifier.
first_30_days: Assemble a test set of real and synthetic images. Build a reverse-lookup against Sentinel-2 and Landsat. Run free verifications for two commodity-finance firms and one newsroom, then convert one to a paid annual license.

title: Model-Swap Regression Service for Contractors
one_liner: Automated testing and porting that lets defense contractors re-platform their AI workflows to a different model vendor in weeks without losing quality.
customer: Defense integrators, primes' AI teams and mid-size government contractors whose workflows were tuned around one model family and must now change vendors.
problem: The D.C. Circuit upheld the DoD supply-chain-risk designation of one model vendor on Sept 26, and DoD is moving classified workloads off it by October. Contractors are cutting that vendor's use. Their prompts, agents and evaluation sets were tuned for one model, and nobody can prove a replacement performs equally on their real tasks.
solution: Capture the contractor's existing workflow traces, build a task-specific eval set, run it across Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok and open-weight models, and auto-rewrite prompts and tool schemas to reach parity. Deliver a signed parity report usable as evidence for the government customer.
why_now: The designation is a fresh legal fact with an October deadline. Vendor politics now shape the supply chain, and lawful-use terms differ by vendor. Model swapping is now a compliance event, not an engineering preference.
revenue_model: $40-200K per migration project, then $3-10K per month for continuous cross-vendor regression monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: The designation is not a one-time event. Every future vendor dispute will force the same migration, so the durable product is a standing eval-and-port harness for a politically volatile model market.
first_30_days: Post a fixed-price migration audit at $15K. Contact 15 small integrators and GenAI.mil agent builders through defense AI communities. Reuse one eval harness across clients while keeping each client's data separate.

title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.

title: Independent-Pricing Ledger for Algorithmic Antitrust Risk
one_liner: A neutral logbook beside revenue-management software that proves humans set rents and room rates independently, and doubles as the underwriting file for algorithmic-collusion defense cover.
customer: Mid-size multifamily operators (2k-25k units), hotel groups and self-storage and student-housing operators using shared-pricing algorithms, plus their antitrust counsel and D&O or defense-cost carriers.
problem: The DOJ's RealPage settlement (Nov 2025) bars use of competitors' nonpublic data and alignment of prices. California and New York banned algorithmic rent-setting in Oct 2025. Class actions continue against landlords, not just vendors. Liability turns on whether users set prices independently or rubber-stamped a pooled tool, and on data provenance. Operators cannot produce that evidence, and carriers will not underwrite defense costs without it.
solution: A light ledger fed by exports or APIs from Yardi, RealPage, Entrata, Duetto and similar tools. It records recommended versus adopted price, override reason codes and data-provenance flags. It produces a quarterly 'independence attestation' reviewed by an outside economist, includes a simulator showing the revenue cost of overriding (often small), and packages an underwriting-grade file for defense-cost cover. Design it under counsel's privilege from day one.
why_now: Enforcement plus new state and city laws hit in late 2025 and 2026, and the settlements set monitoring expectations. Mid-market operators are the next wave of defendants and cannot afford bespoke audits. Insurers are simultaneously narrowing AI and antitrust cover.
revenue_model: $1.50-4 per unit per year (about $6-20k for a 5k-unit operator), $10-25k per year for economist attestation, and 10-15% of the defense-cost premium placed.
non_obvious_insight: The legal variable is not the algorithm's accuracy but its acceptance rate and data provenance, and both are just logs. Evidence must exist before the subpoena arrives. The ledger also becomes the first actuarial dataset for algorithmic-antitrust risk, which no carrier has.
first_30_days: Partner with an ex-DOJ or FTC economist and an antitrust boutique. Build CSV-only ingestion for two property-management systems. Approach 10 mid-size operators through a National Apartment Association state affiliate and their counsel. Sell a $7.5k 'independence audit' of the last 12 months of pricing decisions as the entry product, delivered services-first.

title: Stomach-Ready: GLP-1 Protocols for Endoscopy Centers
one_liner: An intake, coaching and point-of-care gastric ultrasound service that stops GLP-1 patients from turning up to endoscopy with a full stomach and getting cancelled on the table.
customer: Independent GI practices and ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) that run 5-30 endoscopies a day, plus anesthesia groups that staff them. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: GLP-1 drugs slow gastric emptying. Studies in 2026 show retained gastric contents in roughly one in five endoscopy patients on the drugs, and some procedures are aborted. Guidance has moved from 'stop the drug for a week' to 'continue it, use a 24-hour clear-liquid diet, do selective gastric ultrasound and communicate across teams'. Centers have no operations layer to run this. Front-desk staff cannot tell who is on which drug, at what dose or when the last injection was. Surprises happen day-of, causing cancelled slots, rebooking, extra anesthesia risk and idle rooms.
solution: A text and portal intake flags GLP-1 users (brand, dose, weekly or daily, last injection date, symptoms). It auto-assigns the guideline-based protocol, sends coaching and adjusts dose timing per the clinician's rules. It flags high-risk patients (dose escalation phase, gastroparesis symptoms) for a 90-second gastric POCUS on the day. A travelling RN sonographer or a trained center nurse does the scan with a handheld device, and the result goes straight into the anesthesia record. Phase 2 adds AI-assisted image reading.
why_now: A April 2026 wave of studies (residual gastric content 'far higher than expected') and updated multi-society guidance made continue-and-modify the new standard, which needs new workflows. Oral Wegovy and orforglipron are about to widen the user base. Procedure centers are squeezed on throughput and cannot afford dark rooms.
revenue_model: $15-30 per GLP-1 patient screened and coached, plus $60-100 per gastric ultrasound performed. Alternatively a flat $500-1,500 per site per month. One avoided aborted case is worth roughly $1k+ in recovered slot revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The expensive problem is not the rare aspiration event, it is aborted cases and scheduling chaos. Guidelines supplied a protocol but nobody supplies the operations layer that knows which day of the week each patient injects. The physician societies are a free distribution channel once a protocol is written up.
first_30_days: Get 2-3 GI ASCs on a free 60-day pilot and measure their baseline aborted and rebooked rate. Have a GI and an anesthesiologist advisor sign off on a protocol drawn from published guidance. Build the intake on Twilio and a simple form. Buy two handheld ultrasound units (about $3-5k each) and contract an RN sonographer for spot coverage. Then convert the pilot sites to paid.

title: Customs-Verified Collateral for Inventory Lenders
one_liner: An API and reporting layer that verifies borrowers' in-transit inventory against ISF, entry, release and liquidation records, so lenders stop financing containers that do not exist.
customer: Inventory-finance and revenue-based lenders for e-commerce brands, factoring companies, ABL desks at small banks, and buyers of tariff-refund receivables. They pay per verification and per monitored loan.
problem: Lenders finance purchase orders and goods on the water. Their collateral evidence is invoices, a bill of lading PDF and the borrower's word. Fraud, double-pledging, inflated quantities and phantom shipments are a chronic loss driver in small-business trade finance. Tariffs made it worse: duties now consume a big share of landed cost, so lenders need to know what was actually declared, at what value, and whether it cleared or is held. The truth exists in CBP data that brokers see within hours. Lenders see it, if at all, weeks late through the borrower.
solution: Connect to the collateral through consent-based data paths: importer-scheduled ACE reports forwarded to a dedicated inbox, and ABI/status feeds from cooperating brokers that get paid for sharing. Reconcile each financed PO against ISF filing, entry summary, release or hold status, declared value and HTS, and (after the IEEPA ruling) refund eligibility. Deliver a loan-level 'entry-verified' status and exception alerts, such as a container that never had an ISF, a value mismatch, or an exam hold that makes collateral illiquid. The same engine verifies IEEPA refund claims for lenders advancing against them.
why_now: Inventory financing and tariff-duty financing for e-commerce brands surged in 2024-26, and lenders are absorbing losses they do not yet understand. Refund-backed lending is new since the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling and CAPE, and it needs entry-level verification. ACE reports are self-serve, so no permission from CBP is needed. Brokers are looking for revenue beyond thin filing fees.
revenue_model: $15-40 per shipment verification, or a monitoring SaaS fee of about 5-15 basis points on funded volume, with platform minimums of $2-5k a month. Brokers get a revenue share on data feeds. Add-on: refund-claim diligence packages.
non_obvious_insight: A PO and a bill of lading are easy to forge. An ISF filed before vessel loading, tied to a bond, followed by a release message from CBP, is not. It is the closest thing to a government-attested proof that goods exist and are moving. Because the importer owns the ACE data, no data-broker licensing fight is needed. Trade-finance software vendors model documents. Nobody models the entry record.
first_30_days: Approach five small inventory lenders, factors and refund-claim buyers with a manual pilot: they send 10 borrowers' entry data, and you return verified and unverified lists within 48 hours. Recruit two friendly customs brokers for feed access on consenting clients. Build the reconciliation on spreadsheets and scripts first, and charge $500-$1,500 per pilot batch. The first paid lender contract is usually a covenant addition: 'borrower must forward ACE reports monthly'.

title: ILIT Rescue After the Estate-Tax Cliff Disappeared
one_liner: A paid, documented review of irrevocable life insurance trusts built to pay estate tax that most families will never owe.
customer: Trustees (individuals and bank or trust companies), estate attorneys, and families holding ILITs with policies of $1M-$25M.
problem: For decades planners sold ILITs to fund federal estate tax. With the reported $15M-per-person exemption from 2026 (verify), many of these families will never owe it. Trusts keep paying premiums on policies that may be unnecessary, underfunded or poorly performing. Trustees fear fiduciary liability for doing nothing, yet nobody is paid to run the review.
solution: A 'trust-policy triage' service. Ingest the trust document and in-force illustration, classify the trust's purpose, and produce a decision memo: keep, reduce, 1035-exchange, sell, decant or terminate. It documents a prudent-process file for the trustee. Then execute through licensed partners (settlement broker, insurance agency, trust counsel).
why_now: The 2025 tax law reportedly raised and indexed the exclusion. About 10M life policies lapse per year (per the brief's cited market data), and the life-settlement market has active buyers (Coventry, Abacus). Wealth flows to heirs are large enough that leaving policy value on the table is now visible.
revenue_model: $2,500-$7,500 review fee per trust plus success fees on settled or exchanged policies where licensing allows.
non_obvious_insight: Fiduciary duty turns optimization into a mandatory review: trustees are exposed if they do nothing, so someone must be paid to produce the file even when the answer is 'keep'.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 estate attorneys and a licensed life-settlement broker. Pitch corporate trustees' special-assets desks. Run 10 reviews at a $1,500 intro price and learn which outcomes come up most.

title: WhatsApp Tandas With Credit Reporting
one_liner: Felix proved WhatsApp-native finance at $8B of volume. Wrap the rotating savings groups that immigrant households already run in group chats with escrow, default cover and credit reporting.
customer: Latino, West African, Caribbean and South Asian households running tandas, susus and chit-fund-style rotating savings groups. The FDIC's 2023 survey counts 5.6M unbanked and 19M underbanked households, with minimum balances the top barrier.
problem: Rotating savings groups are the real financial system for many households, but they run on cash and trust, one bad organizer or defaulter breaks the pot, and the on-time payment history is invisible to credit bureaus. Cash-funded remittances now carry a 1% federal tax, nudging cash economies toward digital.
solution: A WhatsApp bot to create a tanda (amounts, order, schedule). Contributions are held in a partner-bank pass-through balance, or in stablecoin where appropriate, and payouts release on schedule. The organizer earns a fee, and a small guarantee pool covers late payers. On-time contributions are reported to bureaus as installment history through a furnisher partner.
why_now: Felix reached $8B cumulative volume with revenue up 2.5x on WhatsApp, the remittance tax pushes cash users to digital rails (Forbes, 2026-07-17), and stablecoin and bank-partner rails make small-balance escrow cheap.
revenue_model: 1-2% fee on each pot, $5 per month credit-building subscription, and lender referral fees for graduated members.
non_obvious_insight: Don't replace the tanda, wrap it. The organizer is a trusted social underwriter with better default data than any bureau. The pooled payment history of organized groups becomes a proprietary dataset lenders will pay for.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 organizers via Spanish-language WhatsApp and Facebook groups, churches, taquerias and community organizations. Run 10 pilot tandas with manual escrow in a partner-bank sub-account at a 1.5% fee, and validate the credit-reporting path with a furnisher.

title: Teleoperated Trenching Crews for Infill Lots
one_liner: A control room of remote operators driving retrofitted compact excavators and skid steers on residential lots (utility trenching, pad grading, backfill), sold per linear foot.
customer: Small and ADU builders, factory-built home dealers needing site work, and small site-work contractors short on operators.
problem: Site work and foundations are the first constraint (foundations wait 30+ days; 15-20 houses stuck on foundations for 6+ weeks). Operators are aging out and are poached by larger jobs. Small residential jobs waste an operator's day on travel and waiting.
solution: Rental compact excavators fitted with joystick actuation, cameras, cellular or satellite bonding and a geofence kill-switch. Operators, including 55+ or injured veterans, run machines from a control room, one job after another across a metro, while a local machine tender handles spotting and moves. Start with the lowest-risk tasks in fenced residential lots and sell by linear foot.
why_now: Teleoperation retrofit kits and satellite or 5G links are now off-the-shelf. Autonomous pile drivers already work commercially on solar sites, proving field-robot acceptance. Enforcement and the labor squeeze are thinning site crews.
revenue_model: $175-225 per operated machine-hour or per-linear-foot pricing. Retrofit and rental margin. Later, software licensing to sitework contractors.
non_obvious_insight: The unlock is not autonomy, which is hard, but operator pooling. A person on site wastes half a day traveling and idling, whereas a remote operator can serve many small jobs, and older or injured operators can keep working. Small lots become profitable.
first_30_days: Rent one compact excavator and buy a retrofit or factory remote kit. Test in a closed lot with a safety case and insurance broker input. Sign 3 ADU or factory-home dealers for trenching on fenced lots. Run the first paid jobs with a spotter present.

title: Satiety Peptides for Small-Portion Foods
one_liner: Screen food-grade peptides that trigger the body's own GLP-1 release and put them in high-protein snacks.
customer: Protein bar, yogurt and snack brands serving GLP-1 users and people coming off the drugs.
problem: Small-portion products leave consumers unsatisfied, and CPG incumbents lack anything that helps portions feel sufficient.
solution: ML-screened protein hydrolysate peptides verified in enteroendocrine cell assays for GLP-1 secretion, supplied as an ingredient with structure-function claims only.
why_now: About 12% of Americans use GLP-1s, snack volume is shifting, and AI peptide prediction plus cheap CRO assays let a small team screen quickly.
revenue_model: Ingredient supply and licensing with per-kg pricing and development fees.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 drugs created a mass vocabulary for satiety, so food can compete at the margins of lower-dose and post-drug users without making any drug claim.
first_30_days: Hydrolyze two cheap protein streams, run an in vitro GLP-1 secretion assay through a CRO, and sample results to five snack brands.

title: Master-Leased Housing to Recruit Care Workers Domestically
one_liner: Asset-light staff housing near care facilities that lets operators recruit domestic workers from a wider radius, starting with stranded worker apartments.
customer: Nursing homes, assisted-living and memory-care operators (5-40 sites) and home-care agencies in tight labor markets such as Wisconsin and rural areas.
problem: The visa pause cuts off the overseas pipeline. Direct care workers are paid little (66% earn under $35k), so domestic recruits can't afford to relocate to where beds are staffed. Closed beds and wings in Wisconsin show the cost. Turnover of 77-80% means every hire has to be retained.
solution: Master-lease or take over apartments near facilities, furnish them, and sublease bed by bed to employees at below-market rent. Employers fund the gap ($300-600 per bed per month) under a guarantee. Add a 3-month 'landing pad' with transport, CNA certification and ESL classes, and a relocation pipeline from oversupplied labor markets (laid-off retail and hospitality workers).
why_now: Wisconsin nursing homes spent $100k+ on apartments for overseas workers and then abandoned the plan when visa access closed, so there are stranded assets to take over. About 350,000 Haitians lost TPS on Aug 4, and about one in five immigrant direct-care workers come from countries hit by the 75-country visa pause.
revenue_model: Per-bed monthly management margin ($100-200 on top of rent), employer subsidy, and a $1,500 placement fee per hire retained at 90 days.
non_obvious_insight: When foreign labor is cut off, housing rather than wages becomes the binding constraint to domestic recruitment. A 20-bed closed wing loses over $1M a year in revenue, so a $7k a year housing subsidy per worker is trivially worth it.
first_30_days: Approach the Wisconsin operators who bought apartments and offer to operate and re-let them to domestic hires. Run a 12-bed pilot in one town with two operators and track time-to-fill and 90-day retention.

title: Asset Provenance Ledger for AI Disclosure
one_liner: A plugin for Blender, Photoshop, Unity and Unreal that logs where each asset came from (human-made, AI-generated, purchased) and exports evidence for Steam disclosure and award eligibility.
customer: Indie and mid-size studios (5-100 staff) shipping on Steam, and awards and festival organizers who must adjudicate AI use.
problem: Clair Obscur lost two Indie Game Awards over AI placeholder textures removed before shipping. Eurogamer scored ARC Raiders 2/5 partly over AI voices. Valve requires AI disclosure on Steam. Accusations arrive after launch and the accused have no evidence trail either way.
solution: A local-first logger records per-asset origin (DCC commit hooks, generative-tool API logs, asset-store IDs) into a signed hash chain. It exports an AI Disclosure Report for Steam, award submissions and press, and offers a verifier portal for juries and a public provenance page.
why_now: Award controversies and press scoring now turn on AI use. Steam's disclosure requirement is in force. EA's owners plan AI throughout operations, which will multiply cases.
revenue_model: $15-49 per seat per month, $2-5k per event for awards verification, and $3-10k for forensic audits of accused studios.
non_obvious_insight: The dispute is not AI versus human, it is evidence asymmetry: accusers need no proof and the accused have none. A provenance log protects studios that use AI legitimately (placeholders, disclosed tools) as much as those that do not.
first_30_days: Ship a minimal Blender, Photoshop and Unity logger. Offer it free to awards-eligible entries. Talk to organizers of two indie awards about a verifier pilot, and onboard 20 studios.

title: Medicaid Exemption Evidence Packs for FQHCs
one_liner: An EHR-connected engine that packages state-accepted exemption evidence (medically frail, SUD treatment, disability) so providers keep patients enrolled.
customer: FQHCs, safety-net hospitals and Medicaid MCOs in the 41 expansion states.
problem: Work requirements start Jan 1, 2027 (80 hours a month). Self-attestation is allowed only in 2027 and documentation tightens Jan 1, 2028, with 5.5-6.3M projected coverage losses and a 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hit for hospitals in expansion states. Clinical exemption evidence sits in provider EHRs but nobody packages it for state portals.
solution: Identify likely-exempt patients from problem lists and encounters, generate state-specific attestation and documentation packets, track renewal and verification dates, and give financial counselors a dashboard and patient outreach texts. Wedge is the clinical side, not the state's income-and-hours verification.
why_now: The CMS final rule and state notice deadlines (Aug 31, 2026) are done and system build is underway, so providers have about 3 months of runway. Patient-facing startups exist, but provider-side exemption evidence is mostly open.
revenue_model: $3-8 per covered high-risk member per month, or $75-150 success fee per retained member (an FQHC visit under PPS pays far more than a sliding-fee uninsured visit).
non_obvious_insight: States and their vendors handle income and hours data. The medically-frail and treatment-participation evidence lives with providers, and each retained Medicaid patient is worth many times the fee.
first_30_days: Sign 3 FQHCs in one state through the primary-care association. Manually pull 500 patients' problem lists and produce exemption packets. Measure approval rates, then automate state by state.
